detail.abstract: This paper examines how U.S. mutual funds navigate the intersection of corporate governance and geopolitics by analyzing proxy voting on Chinese corporate charter amendments that formalize Chinese Communist Party (CCP) committees. Using 24,556 fund-level voting records from 2018 to 2022, the study documents a pronounced divergence among the Big Three asset managers. While Vanguard and State Street largely follow proxy advisor recommendations to oppose the institutionalization of CCP committees, BlackRock supports these amendments in 74.70 percent of cases and is more likely to support state-owned, cross-listed, more profitable, and lower-leveraged firms. This "BlackRock exceptionalism" is not explained by firm valuation; instead, the pattern is consistent with using proxy voting as a strategic tool to enhance prospects for regulatory approval and, ultimately, to obtain the first wholly foreign-owned mutual fund license in China. These findings highlight underexplored incentive misalignments among asset managers' commercial interests, fiduciary obligations, and broader U.S. policy objectives.

title: Screening Frontiers

detail.title: Screening Frontiers
detail.abstract: A principal screens an agent with an arbitrary set of allocations X. The agent's preferences over allocations are comonotonic. A subset of allocations X*⊆X is a surplus-elasticity frontier if (i) any other allocation has a demand curve that is pointwise lower and less elastic than some allocation in X* and (ii) the allocations in X* can be ordered in terms of their demand curves such that a higher demand curve is more inelastic. We show that any surplus-elasticity frontier is an optimal menu. Moreover, if the incremental demand curves along the frontier are also ordered by their elasticities, then the frontier is optimal even among stochastic mechanisms. The result is agnostic to type distributions and redistributive welfare weights---the same frontier remains optimal for a broad class of objectives. As applications, we show how these results immediately yield new insights into optimal bundling, optimal taxation, sequential screening, selling information, and regulating a data-rich monopolist.

title: Do Institutional Investors Trade on Covenant Violations?
affiliations: New York University - Leonard N. Stern School of Business, Frankfurt School of Finance & Management and Frankfurt School of Finance & Management

detail.title: Do Institutional Investors Trade on Covenant Violations?
detail.abstract: We develop CovenantAI, an artificial intelligence-powered covenant monitoring methodology, to examine whether institutional investors strategically trade around covenant violations in leveraged loan markets. We document a persistent decline in loan prices during the 100 days preceding violations, with a most pronounced drop 80 days prior to the violation: for example, we find cumulative abnormal returns of -6.39% during the [-80,-60] event window. Price effects are most severe for loans amended post-violation or those that remain in technical default. Covenant violations significantly increase the likelihood that the firm's credit rating is downgraded or the company enters bankruptcy, particularly among non-investment-grade loans held by Collateralized Loan Obligations (CLOs). We document substantial cross-sectional heterogeneity in CLO constraints driven by overcollateralization ratios and CCC-rated loan holdings. Loans predominantly owned by constrained CLOs exhibit steeper pre-violation price declines and significantly more negative abnormal returns. Our evidence demonstrates that constrained institutional investors preemptively divest loan positions in anticipation of covenant violations, with trading intensity reflecting both violation severity and investor-specific portfolio constraints.

title: The Dynamic Integrated Capitalism Model (DICM) A Unified Optimal Control Framework for the Stable Lifetime of Capitalism
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Dynamic Integrated Capitalism Model (DICM) A Unified Optimal Control Framework for the Stable Lifetime of Capitalism
detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Dynamic Integrated Capitalism Model (DICM), a unified optimal-control framework that endogenously determines the remaining stable lifetime of capitalism as an outcome of debt accumulation. Capitalism operates only under the natural inequality: R > g > i > 0 where R denotes the return on capital, g the economic growth rate, and i the policy interest rate. We introduce policy freedom α(D), a decreasing function of total debt D, which constrains the feasible range of monetary policy. As debt accumulates, policy freedom erodes endogenously, eventually preventing the maintenance of g > i and triggering structural collapse̶without reliance on exogenous shocks, political failures, or market irrationality. Using Bellman dynamic programming and Hamiltonian optimal control, we derive the optimal interest-rate path i*(t) that maximizes the duration of R > g > i > 0. DICM integrates macro-level natural laws, meso-level firm investment incentives, and micro-level household carry behavior into a single dynamic system. This paper presents the first framework to quantify capitalismʼs finite stable lifespan as a structurally determined outcome of debt dynamics.

title: Predatory Practices in the UK CV Writing Market: Sales Funnels, Consumer Harm, and Military Targeting

detail.title: Predatory Practices in the UK CV Writing Market: Sales Funnels, Consumer Harm, and Military Targeting
detail.abstract: This paper examines predatory commercial practices in the United Kingdom CV writing market. The focus covers legal context, behavioural manipulation, and heightened exposure for service leavers. Evidence from regulators, platform safety reporting, and consumer narratives indicates that a portion of the sector operates less as a writing service and more as a conversion system. Common patterns include free entry offers used for lead capture, pressured upselling into premium bundles, use of manufactured trust signals, and re use of contact data for ongoing marketing. Market conditions amplify risk because quality is difficult to judge at purchase stage, and buyers often act under stress. The paper maps these patterns to UK consumer protection rules, marketing standards, and data protection guidance, then proposes a due diligence framework that is usable by the public. A dedicated section addresses military and veteran audiences, including why this cohort is repeatedly targeted and how official free support is often bypassed. The paper concludes with recommendations for regulators, platforms, commissioning bodies, charities, and consumers.

detail.abstract: Leveraging variation in robot adoption across U.S. metropolitan areas, we document that automation reduces the sensitivity of inflation to unemployment. To rationalize this finding, we build a New Keynesian model with search frictions in the labor market where robot adoption flattens the Phillips curve. The key channel is the option value of automation: the threat of automating labor tasks alters workers’ effective bargaining power, muting the wage sensitivity to unemployment. We validate the relevance of this channel in the data by showing that robot adoption reduces the sensitivity of inflation to unemployment relatively more in highly unionized metropolitan areas.

title: Hate Crime or Bullying? The High Cost of Framing Harm Among Youth (forthcoming 2027)
affiliations: and

detail.title: Hate Crime or Bullying? The High Cost of Framing Harm Among Youth (forthcoming 2027)

publicationDetails.detailsText: 113 Va. L. Rev. (forthcoming 2027)

detail.abstract: This Article critically examines the growing trend of framing identity-related harm among youth as hate crimes and analyzes the profound consequences of this discursive shift. We argue that categorizing youth behavior as hate crimes instead of another frame such as bullying is not based on objective features of the behavior itself but rather reflects political and social motivations that assign different meanings to similar actions. While the bullying frame contextualizes harmful behavior within developmental and socioecological frameworks, it has become conceptually overbroad and deeply entangled with zero-tolerance and exclusionary school discipline. The hate crime frame goes further, portraying youth as extremists deserving harsh criminal punishment, effectively stripping them of their status as children. Drawing on legal analysis, case studies, constitutional jurisprudence on juvenile culpability, and interdisciplinary scholarship, we demonstrate how the hate crime frame not only normalizes criminal legal interventions for youth but disproportionately harms the very populations it purports to protect—particularly LGBTQ+ youth and youth of color. We further show how the institutionalization of the hate crime frame in schools intensifies racialized criminalization and narrows the space for educational and restorative responses. Rather than advocating for clearer delineations between hate crimes and bullying, we argue for critically reevaluating the appropriateness of applying the hate crime frame to children at all, reject the bullying frame as an adequate alternative, and propose reimagining our approach to youth identity-related harm in ways that acknowledge developmental contexts, address root causes of prejudice, and recognize that young people are not disposable.

detail.title: Microfinance Initiatives for Socio-Economic
detail.abstract: Globally, microfinance has become a powerful tool for empowering marginalised populations and promoting financial inclusion. This study examines the function of microfinance programmes under Kerala Bank's purview. Kerala Bank is an organisation that aims to transform financial services and advance socioeconomic justice in Kerala, India. The study investigates the theoretical foundations and empirical data pertaining to microfinance's effects on poverty reduction, women's empowerment, and grassroots development through an extensive examination of the literature. Based on primary data gathered via surveys, interviews, and case studies, the study evaluates the execution and results of microfinance initiatives supported by Kerala Bank. It evaluates the effectiveness, accessibility, and reach of microfinance interventions in meeting the diverse needs of marginalized groups in Kerala's socioeconomic environment, including small-scale business owners, farmers, and women-led households. The study investigates the links between microfinance programmes and broader development goals such as poverty eradication, gender equality, and community resilience. It investigates how microfinance can help marginalised people in Kerala develop their entrepreneurial spirit, increase their social capital, and pave the way for sustainable lives. This study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of the dynamics influencing microfinance projects within the context of Kerala Bank by critically synthesising actual facts and theoretical perspectives. Policymakers, practitioners, and stakeholders involved in the design and implementation of inclusive financial policies would benefit greatly from the findings' implications in order to fully realise microfinance's transformative potential for equitable development in Kerala and beyond.

detail.abstract: This paper documents bachelor’s degree completion patterns following the launch of ChatGPT. Controlling for school-level shocks, event-study estimates show that by 2024 the number of degrees conferred in programs associated with high occupational AI exposure increases by 5% relative to programs associated with low occupational AI exposure. Programs linked to occupations where AI is more likely to automate tasks also experience a significant increase in bachelor’s degrees conferred. This increase is most pronounced at public and R1 institutions. These findings complement existing studies of AI’s employment effects and provide a more comprehensive understanding of AI’s impact on young workers.

detail.abstract: When humans encounter harmful events, they face a compression problem: rich, multidimensional causal information must be reduced to a small number of interpretive tokens in order to act. This paper argues that moral blame is best understood not as a judgment of character but as a compression schema, a codebook selected under bounded cognitive rate. We introduce a rate-distortion framework for moral attribution and compare two competing codebooks: (A) the moral blame codebook and (B) a threat-response codebook. We argue that at equivalent compression rates, the threat-response codebook yields lower distortion with respect to short-horizon behavioral dynamics while maintaining comparable cognitive economy. Critically, we demonstrate that expansion-only interventions (removing blame without installing a replacement) increase interpretive entropy under threat, predicting destabilization rather than clarity. Three experimental studies are proposed to test these claims. The framework carries no exculpatory implication: mechanism attribution is analytically distinct from moral verdict, responsibility assignment, or boundary enforcement.

detail.abstract: The philosophical underpinnings of cultural influence on food use and preference formulates the basis of this study. Food philosophy primarily entails how food is used and understood in a society. Colonialism affected many African societies through acculturation, forced displacements and the disruption of traditional food systems. South African communities are no exception to the impacts of colonialism. This is evident in the perpetual effects and remnants of settler colonial tendencies in the food systems and land reform areas which continue to shape their foodways. Moreover, African cultural food praxes remain an underserved area in contemporary philosophical and policy formulation debates and research. The study relied on secondary data acquired from academic journals, books, reports, webinars and websites. Literature review was conducted on these keywords and themes: culture, food philosophy, South African settler-colonialism, indigenous food systems, socio-cultural impacts of colonialism as well as South African land and policy reform. title: The Coordination Invariant: Constraint as a Domain-General Control Parameter in Multi-Agent Systems
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Coordination Invariant: Constraint as a Domain-General Control Parameter in Multi-Agent Systems
detail.abstract: Coordination failures across domains are frequently attributed to insufficient information, misaligned incentives, or trust deficits. This paper proposes a structural alternative: persistent coordination in multi-agent systems is governed by the ratio of shared constraint to interpretive variance. Define stability as S = C / V where C is shared constraint, quantified as mutual information (in bits) supplied by publicly observable and mutually legible mechanisms that reduce effective degrees of freedom, and V is interpretive variance, defined as the Shannon entropy over the empirical distribution of agent decision states. In a minimal two-agent repeated coordination simulation, increasing C relative to V produces three regimes: sub-critical (noise-dominated), critical (threshold-sensitive), and super-critical (robust coordination). In the simulated system, super-critical coordination exhibits metastability: after reaching S ≈ 24.5, constraint can be reduced by approximately 40% before coordination collapses. The framework generates testable predictions and explicit falsification criteria. It is consistent with established results in synchronization theory, coordination dynamics, and common-knowledge games. The central implication is structural: under high interpretive variance, shared constraint outperforms equivalent unconstrained information.

title: Measurement as Constraint: Reframing the Observer Problem Without Consciousness
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Measurement as Constraint: Reframing the Observer Problem Without Consciousness
detail.abstract: Quantum mechanics delivers precise predictions for interference, entanglement, and decoherence, yet the mechanism by which quantum superpositions resolve into determinate classical outcomes-the measurement problem-remains conceptually unsettled. Prevailing interpretations invoke conscious observers, proliferating worlds, or decoherence as sufficient explanations, but none adequately account for outcome finality: why a single result becomes stable, irreversible, and shared. This paper reframes measurement not as an act of observation but as a physical constraint that collapses quantum variance into a determinate record. Measurement is defined through four criteria-irreversibility, redundancy, basis selection, and persistence-without reference to consciousness or epistemic access. This constraint-based framework reorganizes existing empirical facts, clarifies the relationship among major interpretations, and yields falsifiable implications, including threshold-dependent regime changes in coherence loss for massive systems. By treating measurement as a variance-to-constraint transition, the approach resolves long-standing concerns about observer dependence through structural mechanics rather than metaphysical assumptions.

detail.abstract: Aim: This study aims to present the potential contribution of Machobane Farming System (MFS) to the adaptation of indigenous communities against unreliable climate shocks and socioeconomic disparities. The primary objectives include awareness on the use and benefits of indigenous agricultural extension models as well as the potential of MFS against climate change and socio-ecological challenges. Background: MFS is a holistic approach to the appropriation and use of natural resources, which improves conservation agriculture, indigenous agriculture, agroforestry and soil health, it extends to farming techniques and food systems. It is a philosophical, socioeconomic and livelihood development model that integrates indigenous and modern farming practices for maximal yield output. Problem: The current climate unreliability and unprecedented inconsistencies continue to affect indigenous agricultural practices, cultural heritage, traditional foodways and food systems. Additionally, the benefits of MFS in agriculture are not well known, this extends to lack of awareness, policy and funding support, as well as physical and mechanical expertise. Methods: A scoping review was used to gather, organize and interpret secondary data such as books, book chapters, case studies, journal articles and reports from websites such as Google scholar, JSTOR, Springer and Sustainability Journal etc. Literature search was conducted on these keywords and themes: Machobane farming system, farming in Lesotho, extension agriculture, indigenous agriculture, climate change, food security, water conservation and land management. Findings: MFS enhances food availability and diversity as well as access to food producing resources for indigenous communities. Principles of MFS encompass enhanced soil health, water conservation and land management-through rainwater collection, less external input, and pest management by smallholder farmers. Moreover, MFS has the potential to improve agricultural resources, food security and biodiversity management. Contribution: The author seeks to raise awareness on the relevance and significance indigenous agricultural extensions through the lens of MFS. This method may be beneficial to indigenous communities, resulting in improved rural livelihoods, enhanced crop yields, improved food security and food systems, less environmental impact and minimal land degradation-through techniques such as likoti (holes) and matsema (communal labour).

title: The Net Present Value of the Billionaire Tax Act: An Assessment of the Fiscal Effects of California's Proposed Wealth Tax
affiliations: Stanford University - Hoover Institution, Stanford Graduate School of Business, , Stanford University - Hoover Institution and

detail.title: The Net Present Value of the Billionaire Tax Act: An Assessment of the Fiscal Effects of California's Proposed Wealth Tax
detail.abstract: This report examines the revenue and migration impact of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5 percent tax on the worldwide net worth of individuals exceeding $1 billion. Using data from the 2025 Forbes Billionaire List, news reports detailing the residential real estate holdings of California billionaires, and public announcements of billionaire departures from the state, we estimate the behavioral response and associated revenue loss to this new tax using several different methodologies. Even before accounting for reductions in other tax bases such as the income tax, we estimate that the Act will collect approximately $40 billion, less than half of the $100 billion projected by proponents.  This range accounts for the publicly confirmed taxpayer migration that have already eliminated nearly 30% of the Act's wealth tax base and uses the wealth tax base elasticity literature to predict the additional tax base losses attributable to unannounced, stealth departures. We estimate that California's billionaires contribute $3.3-5.8 billion annually in state income taxes. The present value of permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than fully offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $24.7 billion. Across 100,000 simulated revenue and discount rate combinations, 71% of plausible outcomes produce a negative net present value of state revenues. Finally, we note that policies that distort behavior but generate little or no net revenue gain are not harmless as they may nonetheless impose substantial costs on residents through reduced employment, investment, and income.

title: Exploring the Uncharted World of Audit Institutions

detail.title: Exploring the Uncharted World of Audit Institutions

publicationDetails.detailsText: Comparative Administrative Law New Voices, New Perspectives, Edited by Peter L. Lindseth, Mariana Mota Prado, Blake Emerson, Farrah Ahmed, and Megan Pfiffer

detail.abstract: External auditors of the executive branch, commonly known as Supreme Audit Institutions, have quietly emerged as some of the most consequential yet least examined actors in contemporary administrative states. Once confined to financial oversight, they now often scrutinize public policy, shape government decision-making, and in some cases even pre-empt or override the actions of elected officials. This chapter addresses their puzzling absence from comparative legal scholarship and charts a new course for their study. It critically unpacks the typologies that dominate existing analyses, exposes their explanatory limitations, and shows how the expanding mandates and ancillary roles of these institutions are redefining the boundaries between financial oversight and constitutional accountability. The chapter also draws on different national experiences to suggest that some of these institutions are also increasingly straddling the line between providing technocratic oversight and encroaching on government decision-making.

title: 'Home to Me Has Been Mostly Just a Backpack': Childhood Housing Instability Among Survivors of Sex Trafficking

detail.title: 'Home to Me Has Been Mostly Just a Backpack': Childhood Housing Instability Among Survivors of Sex Trafficking
detail.abstract:
Background: Sex trafficking survivors face significant barriers to stable housing, which is essential for healing. Research on housing instability remains limited, especially that which reflects the lived experiences of survivors of sex trafficking. 

Objective: Given limited research on housing and sex trafficking, this study explored how childhood housing instability intersects with other vulnerabilities to shape pathways into sex trafficking in the United States. Participants and Setting: Twenty-three adult women survivors participated in a 1-hour semi-structured Zoom interview between November and December 2024. 

Methods: Recruitment involved purposive and snowball sampling. All interviews were recorded and transcribed. Data analysis involved constant comparative analysis and consisted of repeated readings of data, coding, and creation of themes and categories. Results: Findings revealed that 73.9% (n = 17) of participants experienced housing instability during childhood, often linked to poverty, abuse, and involvement in the child welfare system. Many faced continued instability into adulthood, increasing vulnerability to trafficking. Participants described harmful experiences in foster care and group homes, with some trafficked by caregivers. Stable housing was identified as a critical need. 

Conclusions: Housing instability is a key social determinant of trafficking vulnerability. Survivor-informed housing interventions must prioritize safety, autonomy, and trauma-informed care. Cross-sector collaboration and systemic reforms in child welfare and housing policy are essential to prevent exploitation and support healing.

detail.abstract: Religious conversion of Hindu women to Islam in Kerala, situated in the southern most part of India, has emerged as a significant social problem, often associated with political, gendered, and security concerns. This article explores the conversion process, analyzing the socio-cultural and religious implications, and its connection to radicalization, terrorism, and overall global security. By applying Foucault's power theory, constructivism, liberalism, neorealism, and feminist theories, this article provides a ground for understanding how the conversion process impacts women's identities and their roles and how it is related to global terrorism. detail.abstract: The Total Portfolio Approach and Strategic Asset Allocation are widely viewed as competing frameworks for institutional portfolio management. We argue they differ in a single governance parameter: the tracking error constraint. Using U.S. equity and bond data from 2000 to 2026, with portfolio simulations spanning 2004 to 2026, we show that Sharpe ratios are statistically indistinguishable across the full constraint spectrum while the volatility of realized tracking error varies approximately 12-fold. The cost of constraints spikes during crises, when forward returns are richest and governance pressure to de-risk is strongest. Dynamic tracking error subsumes both approaches and provides boards with a more productive framework for investment governance.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the effects of fiscal policy announcements on household expecta-tions. We document announcements of price-related expansionary fiscal measures in response to the cost-of-living crisis in the four largest euro area economies and exploit the exogenous timing of fiscal actions relative to household survey participation to estimate their causal effects. Following fiscal announcements, households revise their beliefs: inflation perceptions rise, and unemployment perceptions fall. The latter effect persists into short-run unemployment expectations, while inflation expectations remain unchanged, suggesting households perceived inflationary pressures as temporary. These results suggest a significant signaling channel of fiscal policy, as fiscal announcements reveal information about the underlying economic conditions and the government’s commitment to stabilization. We rationalize these findings through a general equilibrium New Keynesian model extended with information frictions and an inflation-stabilizing role for fiscal policy. The model isolates the informational content of fiscal policy and shows that belief revisions are consistent with demand-driven dynamics.

title: Zones of Independence at the National Labor Relations Board After Humphrey's Executor
affiliations: George Washington University Law School

detail.title: Zones of Independence at the National Labor Relations Board After Humphrey's Executor

publicationDetails.journalName: George Washington University Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In 1935, Congress established the National Labor Relations Board independent of any cabinet department to resolve labor conflict and protected its members from at-will removal to ensure impartial and expert adjudication. Now, the unitary executive is en vogue. The President has fired a Board member without cause, the Supreme Court has suggested that the NLRB’s removal protections may be coming to an end, and Congress doesn’t seem to mind. Proponents of an independent NLRB have warned that subjecting members to the President’s removal authority encourages White House interference in the disposition of individual labor disputes.

This Article, however, contends that the Constitution’s Due Process Clause erects zones of independence that wall off the Board’s adjudication from the pressure of the Executive. In numerous contexts, the courts have long recognized that excessive political interference in administrative adjudication violates parties’ rights to due process of law and an impartial tribunal. The influence of politics must end at the courthouse steps. While the end of removal protections for the Board members brings with it significant negative consequences, which the Article discusses, the potential demise of the independent agency does not necessarily mean the end of adjudicative independence for workers relying on the NLRB to protect their rights under the law.

title: When Should the Legal System Help Redistribute Income?
affiliations: University of Chicago - Law School and Yale University - Law School

detail.title: When Should the Legal System Help Redistribute Income?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Yale Law School, Public Law Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Yale Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In this Essay, we consider when legal rules should be efficient and when they should not. We focus on conditions that can cause the socially optimal legal rule to diverge from the efficient legal rule—i.e., the legal rule that would be optimal absent distributional considerations. These conditions include preferences or behaviors that vary over the income distribution, imperfect salience of the incentives generated by legal rules, income tax evasion or avoidance, and regulated activities that generate income. Like the general argument for efficient legal rules, all of these exceptions draw on existing results from the economics literature on optimal taxation. Our goal is to translate these arguments to settings where the question of interest relates to the design of a legal rule rather than, say, the design of a commodity tax. In particular, we seek to clarify the types of arguments that can support the adoption of inefficient legal rules when income taxation is available as a policy tool.

In addition to canvassing conditions that can invalidate the conclusion that legal rules should be efficient when all policy tools are available, we also highlight several real-world institutional and political factors that can make redistribution through legal rules less or more desirable.

title: The Top 100 Legal Scholars of 2025

detail.title: The Top 100 Legal Scholars of 2025
detail.abstract: Traditional legal scholarship rankings rely almost exclusively on career-long publication metrics, a method that inherently favors decades-old articles and often obscures the authors producing the most impactful research today. This article presents an alternative: a ranking of the 100 most-cited legal scholars based solely on citations to articles published during a recent three-year window. Now in its third year, the ranking reveals who is writing the most impactful legal scholarship right now, regardless of career stage or institutional pedigree. This year's results feature significant movement: a new law school claims the top institutional spot, a scholar from outside the U.S. News top 100 law schools breaks into the top ten for the first time, and women authors reach a new high of seven seats in the top ten. The article also introduces a co-author-adjusted ranking, examines the characteristics of highly cited articles — finding that longer articles and shorter titles continue to dominate — and offers an early assessment of COVID-19's impact on scholarly productivity. Finally, it provides a candid account of how the authors used AI tools, including Claude and Gemini, in preparing this year's ranking, documenting where AI saved significant time and where it did not.

detail.title: External Debt and Growth Dynamics in Selected West African Countries

publicationDetails.detailsText: UMM Journal of Accounting and Financial Management (UMMJAFM), Volume 5| Issue 2, July 2025

detail.abstract: This study investigates the growth implications of external debt in six selected West African countries Nigeria, Ghana, Mali, Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, and Burkina Faso covering the period 1990-2024. Anchored on a quantitative research design within a dynamic panel framework, the study applies the System Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) to account for endogeneity and dynamic interactions. The population comprises all West African states, while the sample is restricted to the six largest economies, representing over 85% of the region's output. The study relies on secondary data sourced from the World Development Indicators (WDI), covering GDP growth, external debt stock, debt service, and macroeconomic controls. The findings reveal that external debt stock exerts a significant negative effect on economic growth, while debt servicing is positive but statistically insignificant. Real effective exchange rate appreciation further undermines growth, whereas foreign direct investment supports GDP performance. These results highlight the inefficiency of debt utilization and its limited role in stimulating growth dynamics. The study recommends that ECOWAS governments restructure borrowing strategies by linking new debt strictly to growth-enhancing projects, thereby strengthening the capacity of external debt to positively influence long-term growth dynamics in the sub-region.

title: Cross-Agent Governance Alignment (CAGA): A Zero-Knowledge Formalization for Cross-Organizational AI Governance

detail.title: Cross-Agent Governance Alignment (CAGA): A Zero-Knowledge Formalization for Cross-Organizational AI Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of FERZ, Inc., which develops governance architectures related to the research topic discussed in this paper. The paper presents a problem formalization and does not disclose proprietary implementation details.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a theoretical formalization and does not involve human participants, patient data, or animal subjects. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
As autonomous AI agents increasingly coordinate across institutional boundaries in regulated industries, existing governance frameworks prove insufficient. Current models assume either a single organizational authority or full policy transparency between participants—assumptions that do not hold in multi-stakeholder environments where governance constraints encode proprietary risk tolerances, regulatory interpretations, and competitive strategy.

This paper formalizes the Cross-Agent Governance Alignment (CAGA) problem: verifying mutual governance compatibility between agents operating under distinct policy regimes without disclosing those policies. We define governance domains and cross-domain interactions, introduce the governance alignment predicate Φ(Dᵢ, Dⱼ, τ), and formalize the problem under an honest-but-curious threat model appropriate for regulated settings.

We identify the essential properties any valid solution must satisfy, including alignment correctness, policy confidentiality, governance determinism, evidentiary sufficiency, composable security, and forward secrecy of governance state. We then demonstrate that CAGA is irreducible to existing paradigms, including agent communication protocols, federated learning, secure multi-party computation, single-organization governance architectures, and blockchain-based transparency systems.

CAGA is a zero-knowledge coordination problem at the intersection of AI governance, cryptographic protocol design, and multi-agent systems. By precisely defining the problem space and evaluation criteria, this work establishes the foundation for rigorous protocol development while deliberately stopping short of implementation disclosure.

title: Comment to Consumer Financial Protection Bureau on Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Personal Financial Data Rights Reconsideration

detail.title: Comment to Consumer Financial Protection Bureau on Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Personal Financial Data Rights Reconsideration

publicationDetails.detailsText: George Mason Law & Economics Research Paper No. 26-05
publicationDetails.journalName: Antonin Scalia Law School, George Mason University, Law & Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
On August 22, 2025, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau announced an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Personal Financial Data Rights Reconsideration, aka, the “1033 Rulemaking.” This Comment, filed on October 21, 2025, addresses the four questions posed by the CFPB.

This Comment argues that the rulemaking provides an opportunity to enact a regulatory structure that can benefit consumers, competition, innovation, and financial inclusion, especially for consumers historically underserved by the traditional financial system. In addition, by creating an efficient, workable regulatory structure, the rule can increase consumer data privacy and security by eliminating the need for cumbersome workarounds like screen-scraping practices that impose costs on financial institutions and increase the risk of data breaches for consumers.

The Comment starts by observing that the data in question is not “owned” by either consumers or banks but instead is jointly produced by consumers and providers. As a result, instead of focusing on who “owns” the data, regulatory policy should focus on consumer’s decision-making over how their data is used and preventing misuse of their data, instead of unsolvable questions of data “ownership.”

Regarding the four specific questions posed by the CFPB, the Comment advocates for a broad definition of “representative” that includes third-party data aggregators and fintech providers, noting that narrow interpretations ignore the benefits consumers derive from seller-driven competition. It criticizes the high access fees demanded by large banks as a manifestation of an “anticommons” problem designed to extract monopoly rents and stifle rivals, suggesting instead that fees should be limited to marginal costs or ideally remain at a baseline of zero. On the issue of data security, clear, API-based sharing protocols are far safer than the ad hoc workarounds, such as “screen scraping,” that emerge when consumer demand for portability is blocked. Finally, the Comment urges the CFPB to move away from archaic “notice and consent” models toward a “tort approach” that focuses on preventing the actual misuse of information while facilitating legitimate uses that increase consumer welfare.

title: AI-Assisted Economic Measurement from Survey Instruments: Evidence from Public-Employee Pension Choice
affiliations: Stanford University - Hoover Institution and Stanford University - Hoover Institution

detail.title: AI-Assisted Economic Measurement from Survey Instruments: Evidence from Public-Employee Pension Choice
detail.abstract: We develop an iterative framework for economic measurement that leverages large language models to extract measurement structure directly from survey instruments. The approach maps survey items to a sparse distribution over latent constructs through what we term a "soft mapping," aggregates harmonized responses into respondent-level subdimension scores, and disciplines the resulting taxonomy through out-of-sample incremental validity tests and discriminant validity diagnostics. The framework explicitly integrates iteration into the measurement construction process. Overlap and redundancy diagnostics trigger targeted taxonomy refinement and constrained remapping, ensuring that added measurement flexibility is retained only when it delivers stable out-of-sample performance gains. Applied to a large-scale public employee retirement plan survey, the framework identifies which semantic components contain behavioral signal and clarifies the economic mechanisms, such as beliefs versus constraints, that matter for retirement choices. The methodology provides a portable measurement audit of survey instruments that can guide both empirical analysis and survey design.

title: Exploring pathways to achieving climate mitigation goals and the SDGs in Austria: A stakeholder-guided modelling approach
affiliations: BOKU University, Vienna, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Millennium Institute and Universität für Bodenkultur Wien (BOKU)

detail.title: Exploring pathways to achieving climate mitigation goals and the SDGs in Austria: A stakeholder-guided modelling approach
detail.abstract: Addressing climate change and sustainable development remains a persistent global and national challenge. This paper responds to the need for integrated national transformation pathways, informed by a participatory co-creation process. We apply a stakeholder-guided system dynamics modelling approach using the iSD-AT model to analyse two scenarios: a baseline scenario reflecting less ambitious energy and climate policies, and the stakeholder-driven Co-SDG scenario that integrates climate change mitigation goals (SDG13) with other Sustainable Development Goals (particularly SDGs 1, 7, 8, 10 and 12). Translating co-created policy measures into quantitative modelling enabled us to explore an integrated scenario targeting multiple sustainability goals and combining a diverse set of policy measures, including policies rarely represented in quantitative modelling. At the same time, the process revealed important limitations and blind spots of quantitative models, as stakeholders emphasised institutional and governance dimensions that are only partially captured in such frameworks. The Co-SDG scenario results highlight strong interdependencies between economic and environmental dynamics, showing that stabilizing real GDP per capita improves environmental outcomes, including lower greenhouse gas emissions, underscoring the need to rethink the role of economic growth within the SDG framework. Policies primarily targeting social objectives mitigate negative effects associated with lower economic growth. Finally, the analysis highlights the importance of accounting for synergies among interacting policy measures, which evolve and intensify over time, to mitigate unintended adverse effects, particularly over the long term.

title: Pharmaceutical Consumption, Economic Growth And Life Expectancy In The OECD: The Application Of A New Causal Direction From Dependency Algorithm And A Deepnet Process

detail.title: Pharmaceutical Consumption, Economic Growth And Life Expectancy In The OECD: The Application Of A New Causal Direction From Dependency Algorithm And A Deepnet Process
detail.abstract: Purpose-The objective of this study is to reevaluate the correlation among pharmaceutical consumption, per capita income, and life expectancy across different age groups (at birth, middle age, and advanced age) within the OECD countries between 1998 and 2018. Design/methodology/approach-We employ a two-step methodology, utilizing two independent approaches. Firstly, we conduct the Dumitrescu-Hurlin pairwise panel causality test, followed by Machine Learning (ML) experiments employing the Causal Direction from Dependency (D2C) Prediction algorithm and a DeepNet process, thought to deliver robust inferences with respect to the nature, sign, direction, and significance of the causal relationships revealed in the econometric procedure. Findings-Our findings reveal a two-way positive bidirectional causal relationship between GDP and total pharmaceutical sales per capita. This contradicts the conventional notion that health expenditures decrease with economic development due to general health improvements. Furthermore, we observe that GDP per capita positively correlates with life expectancy at birth, 40, and 60, consistently generating positive and statistically significant predictive values. Nonetheless, the value generated by the input life expectancy at 60 on the target income per capita is negative (À 61.89%), shedding light on the asymmetric and nonlinear nature of this nexus.

title: Indigenous Community Preferences for Road Development in Indonesia: Trade-offs Between Accessibility and Forest-Based Livelihoods
affiliations: Padjadjaran University, University of Indonesia, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Indonesia and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Indigenous Community Preferences for Road Development in Indonesia: Trade-offs Between Accessibility and Forest-Based Livelihoods
detail.abstract: Road expansion is widely promoted as a catalyst for rural development, yet in forest frontiers it can also undermine Indigenous livelihoods and culturally salient ecological resources. This paper quantifies how Indigenous Punan communities in Malinau Regency, North Kalimantan, evaluate trade-offs between improved road access and the preservation of livelihood–ecological assets. We implement a discrete choice experiment with 169 Punan respondents from upstream and downstream settlements, comparing preferences across alternatives defined by travel time to the nearest city, per-trip travel cost, expected agarwood income per forest trip, and the condition of salt-lick sites used for hunting. Preferences are estimated using conditional logit and mixed logit models, and translated into marginal willingness to pay and non-monetary marginal rates of substitution. Results indicate that households value reductions in travel time and travel costs, but place substantially larger welfare weight on safeguarding salt-lick sites and forest-based livelihood returns. Avoiding complete loss of a salt-lick site is valued at approximately IDR 9.6–10.1 million per trip, and the implied travel-time reductions needed to offset such loss exceed the maximum time improvements offered in the experiment, suggesting these sites are treated as close to non-compensable cultural–ecological assets. Upstream households exhibit stronger status-quo preferences, consistent with greater livelihood vulnerability. The findings challenge narratives that assume road access is an unconditional public good and underscore the need for infrastructure planning that explicitly incorporates Indigenous preferences and safeguards critical livelihood resources.

title: Ecology and Labour in the Circuit of Capital: Circulation labour and its transformative potential amidst the global environmental crisis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Ecology and Labour in the Circuit of Capital: Circulation labour and its transformative potential amidst the global environmental crisis
detail.abstract: AbstractThe paper develops a conceptual perspective for understanding the role of labour in the global environmental crisis, focusing on the circulation of commodities under capitalism. Building on insights from eco-Marxism and Environmental Labour Studies (ELS), the paper analysis circulation labour (labour that organises, moves, and stores commodities) as a critical yet often overlooked site of both capital accumulation and ecological transformation. Circulation labour shapes the temporal and spatial organisation of global value chains, mediates society-nature relations, and realises surplus value, while simultaneously holding potential for disruptive and transformative action. The paper introduces the notion of ecological chokepoints, sites where concentrated material and energy flows intersect with labour processes, infrastructure, and ecological transformation. The study illustrates how chokepoints condense socio-ecological contradictions and reveal the dual significance of labour: it is essential for maintaining capital circulation and a potential lever for contesting the destructive dynamics of capitalism towards nature. By focussing on labour and the ecological implications of commodity circulation, the proposed analytical lens contributes to Ecological Economics (EE) and critical approaches to socio-ecological transformation, highlighting the importance of investigating the labour process in the transformation of nature and reflecting on labour agency in shaping sustainable futures.

title: Do Storms Bring Crime? Evidence from US counties

detail.title: Do Storms Bring Crime? Evidence from US counties

I also thank participants in the Half-Baked Seminar at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln and the Applied Microeconomics Workshop (2025) at the University of Missouri for valuable comments and feedback.

detail.abstract: Little causal evidence exists regarding the long-term impacts of natural disasters on crime. Using a balanced panel of county-level crime data spanning 1980-2020, this paper estimates the short-and long-run effects of hurricanes of varying intensities that affected U.S. counties between 1990 and 2010. Findings indicate that while minor hurricanes have little effect on crime, major hurricanes cause significant increases in property crime. In the decade following exposure to major hurricanes, property crime rates rise by 8.5% relative to the baseline mean, imposing an estimated per-capita social cost of $120 on treated counties. These effects are largely driven by evacuation orders and selective out-migration in the short run and by declining per-capita incomes in the long run. Furthermore, hurricane effects are disproportionately larger for counties with less disaster experience and lower incomes, which risk losing 1.4% and 2.2% of percapita GDP, respectively, due to hurricane-induced crime. Overall, the findings underscore the need for greater resource allocation toward vulnerable communities and increased investment in disaster resilience measures to mitigate the economic and social consequences of climate change.

title: High Temperatures, Extreme Weather Events, and Fertility in Italy: A Municipal-level Event-Based Analysis
affiliations: University of Padua and University of Padua

detail.title: High Temperatures, Extreme Weather Events, and Fertility in Italy: A Municipal-level Event-Based Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the short-term effects of exceptional climatic episodes on fertility in Italy, distinguishing between extreme monthly average temperatures (measured using Copernicus data) and severe weather events recorded in the European Severe Weather Database (ESWD). We construct a novel municipality-level dataset covering the 2003-2023 period, integrating fertility data with information on climate shocks. To account for the non-random spatial and temporal distribution of climate shocks, we employ an event-study framework combined with propensity score matching, controlling for pre-treatment fertility dynamics and municipality-specific characteristics. The biological lag between conception and birth provides a natural over-identification test, enhancing causal interpretation. Our results show that, once treated municipalities are matched with comparable controls, the estimated effects of both high temperatures and extreme weather events on fertility are small and statistically insignificant. These findings underscore the importance of addressing seasonal confounding in panel analyses and introduce the ESWD into demographic research, enabling the study of short-term demographic responses to extreme climatic events.

title: Gender Quotas and Public Goods Provision: Does the Type of Quota Matter?
affiliations: University of Notre Dame

detail.title: Gender Quotas and Public Goods Provision: Does the Type of Quota Matter?
detail.abstract: Using the implementation of mandatory and voluntary gender quotas for political office in Namibia as natural experiments, I investigate how different types of gender quotas alter the provision of public goods. With a difference-in-differences empirical strategy, I find that the mandatory quota increased public goods provision by 0.19 standard deviations which was driven by increases in schools, health clinics, and paved roads among others. The voluntary quota had an insignificant impact on overall public goods provision. In addition to the increase in public goods provision, the mandatory quota caused perceived corruption of politicians to decrease but had no effect on citizens' trust in the legislature. However, there was a loss in trust of the legislature resulting from the voluntary gender quota suggesting this type of quota may not be a sustainable long-run policy.

title: Rejecting Work Inequality: Women Say “No” to Unequal Workloads or Unequal Earnings?
affiliations: Bryant University and Monash University

detail.title: Rejecting Work Inequality: Women Say “No” to Unequal Workloads or Unequal Earnings?
detail.abstract: Pay inequality can arise from unequal earnings for the same job or an unequal workload for the same earnings. While existing research focuses on aversion to unequal earnings, little is known about aversion to unequal workloads, particularly gender differences. We show that female workers are more willing to accept unequal workload than unequal earnings allocations. By contrast, male workers exhibit similar responses to the workload and earnings inequality. The findings highlight that women's lower aversion to unequal workloads can contribute to the gender earnings gap. Promoting equal workload allocation can be crucial in addressing the gender gap in the labor market.

title: AI and the Labor Market: A Worker's-Eye View
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - Department of Economics,  and Washington University in St. Louis

detail.title: AI and the Labor Market: A Worker's-Eye View

declarations.funderStatement: We gratefully acknowledge financial support from the Weidenbaum Center on the Economy, Government, and Public Policy

detail.abstract: We collect and analyze data from a survey of just under 2,000 U.S. citizens to study perceptions about the role of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the workplace, as well as changes in career-relevant decision-making since the initial launch of ChatGPT. We report four main findings. First, adoption patterns depend on both the perceived effect of AI on current productivity and on its perceived capacity as a career-relevant learning tool, with the latter being slightly more important. Second, most respondents report dedicating more time to learning now compared to before ChatGPT, and this trend is driven by those who believe AI is a useful tool for learning. Third, while time invested in learning tends to decrease with age, this trend is attenuated among who believe in AI's potential as a learning tool. Fourth, workers who believe that AI is a complement to their own effort increase their effort in response to the introduction of AI while workers who believe that AI is a substitute show no such effect. These patterns are robust to the inclusion of a rich set of controls. Our results demonstrate the importance of worker-level tradeoffs in shaping heterogeneous responses to the introduction of AI and highlight career-long learning as a dimension of AI capabilities that is especially important in the eyes of many workers.

title: Market Narratives vs. Fed Views: Generated Forecasting and Their Dispersion
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Students and

detail.title: Market Narratives vs. Fed Views: Generated Forecasting and Their Dispersion
detail.abstract: We construct two text-based measures of monetary-policy expectations by applying Chat-GPT to generate ex ante forecasts of federal funds rate changes from Wall Street Journal articles and FOMC Minutes. Minutes-based forecasts closely track subsequent realized rate changes, whereas market-news-based forecasts are more informative about monetary policy surprises. A parsimonious structural decomposition of the two forecasts implies a nontrivial Fed-specific information component, while the Fed-market forecast wedge loads systematically on macroeconomic fundamentals. We next show that the cross-article dispersion of market-news forecasts captures narrative disagreement rather than aggregate uncertainty. Finally, disagreement affects how financial investors assess the uncertainty around scheduled announcements. In both equity and Treasury markets, VIX predicts pre-FOMC drifts primarily when disagreement is low; when disagreement is high, volatility becomes a less informative proxy for uncertainty and investors instead rely more on policy-relevant fundamentals to anchor expectations. Overall, the results highlight the role of informational frictions and belief dispersion in shaping expectation formation and pre-announcement risk premia.

title: The KAPSARC Energy Model for Saudi Arabia: Documentation of the Model Build Called “KEM-SA_v9.16”
affiliations: King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center (KAPSARC)

detail.title: The KAPSARC Energy Model for Saudi Arabia: Documentation of the Model Build Called “KEM-SA_v9.16”
detail.abstract: The KAPSARC Energy Model for Saudi Arabia is a partial economic equilibrium model that characterizes some of the energy and most energy-intensive sectors in the Saudi economy; these are the electric power, petrochemicals, refining, water desalination, oil and gas upstream and cement sectors. Each sector is contained within its own sub-model and acts as an agent that makes decisions on fuel usage, investment and technology to minimize its cost or maximize profit.

title: Whether to Know the End: Strategic End-Game Ignorance and Cooperation in Repeated Prisoner's Dilemma Games
affiliations: School of Economics, Nankai University and Nankai University - School of Economics

detail.title: Whether to Know the End: Strategic End-Game Ignorance and Cooperation in Repeated Prisoner's Dilemma Games
detail.abstract: This study investigates how strategic ignorance regarding a game's duration can sustain cooperation in finitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games, where cooperation typically collapses due to backward induction. Theoretical subgame-perfect equilibria show that remaining uninformed can maintain cooperation when continuation probabilities are sufficiently high. Lab experiments indicate that while avoiding "horizon information" correlates with higher cooperation, such behavior is rare and unstable; nudges and experience provide only temporary increases. However, avoidance rises substantially when players condition choices on partner behavior. Ultimately, strategic complexity-characterized by coexisting symmetric and asymmetric equilibria and diverging off-equilibrium paths-obstructs the selection of Pareto-improving outcomes.

title: Event Studies in Finance with Dynamic Betas
affiliations: , University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School and UNSW Business School, University of New South Wales

detail.title: Event Studies in Finance with Dynamic Betas
detail.abstract: In this paper we develop short horizon event study methodology, in the presence of time-varying risk, relative to the conventional and widely utilized static risk approach. We propose new methods with realized beta estimators and high frequency intra-day returns that allow for dynamic risk in abnormal return measurement around events, that include for example, multiple announcements. These are relevant not only to the discipline of financial economics and extend more broadly for example, to applications in law and accounting.

title: Kuwait Stock Exchange: Microstructure Reform between Market Maker in 2016 and Qualified Intermediary in 2026
affiliations: Kuwait International Law School

detail.title: Kuwait Stock Exchange: Microstructure Reform between Market Maker in 2016 and Qualified Intermediary in 2026
detail.abstract:
Kuwait Stock Exchange continues, in collaboration with the Capital Markets Authority, to implement a comprehensive development plan to transform the market in both form and substance, aiming to attract greater liquidity, accelerate its movement, and support market capitalization growth.

The microstructure of capital markets consists of two main types: The first is the order-driven market, which relies solely on traders' orders but halts when demand disappears, freezing stock liquidity. The second is the quote-driven market, where the market maker plays a leading role by committing to buy and sell securities at specified prices, ensuring continuous trading activity and enhancing liquidity.

Following the liquidity crisis of 2014, the Exchange launched the market maker program in 2016 to support the execution structure of trading operations. To complete the comprehensive reform, it introduced in 2026 the role of the qualified intermediary, who manages omnibus accounts allowing immediate settlement of transactions without multiple parties. This intermediary holds the registered ownership while actual ownership belongs to clients, achieving unprecedented speed and flexibility in executing and settling operations through unified trading accounts. Thus, the cycle of reforming Kuwait Stock Exchange's microstructure has been completed.

title: Learning, Belief Distortions and Financial Crisis: A Macro-Finance Model with Diagnostic Expectations
affiliations: and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Students

detail.title: Learning, Belief Distortions and Financial Crisis: A Macro-Finance Model with Diagnostic Expectations
detail.abstract: We incorporate learning and diagnostic expectations (DE) into a continuous-time macroeconomic model with financial intermediaries. We show that learning dampens the response to permanent TFP shocks but forces the economy to react to transitory shocks. Learning also generates misjudged crises in which beliefs diverge from the fundamentals. We uncover a stabilization paradox regarding DE. On average, DE exerts a stabilizing force. However, along histories with small realized adverse shocks, DE generates more fragile crises, in which nonlinear dynamics amplify seemingly mild disturbances. A combination of learning and DE can produce the Minsky-style crises, where minor negative shocks after a long period of optimism can trigger disproportionately severe collapses. We use the calibrated model to revisit the 2007-2008 financial crisis and show that it successfully replicates: (1) a pre-crisis period characterized by elevated optimism, compressed risk premia, increased leverage, and a rising credit-to-GDP ratio; and (2) a financial crisis accompanied by a sharp contraction in output.

title: Decoding Trump’s Economic Security Agreements: It’s All About China
affiliations: Singapore Management University - Yong Pung How School of Law

detail.title: Decoding Trump’s Economic Security Agreements: It’s All About China
detail.abstract: This paper examines the emergence of a new category of US trade agreements, beginning with the US–UK Economic Prosperity Deal and extending to recent arrangements with Southeast Asian and Latin American partners. Although these agreements fall short of traditional free trade agreements and are often dismissed as shallow because they do not liberalize substantially all trade, this paper argues that such assessments miss their strategic significance. Precisely because they depart from the FTA model, these agreements illuminate the evolving priorities of US trade policy: the elevation of economic security over liberalization, alignment over reciprocity, and control over efficiency. The paper analyzes the structure and function of these arrangements, showing how they are designed to address the “China shock” indirectly through third countries, and assesses their implications for China, US partners, and the future trajectory of the global trading system.

title: Long-Run Sovereign Debt Composition: An Analytic Ergodic Framework with Explicit Maturity Structure
affiliations: U.S. Department of the Treasury

detail.title: Long-Run Sovereign Debt Composition: An Analytic Ergodic Framework with Explicit Maturity Structure
detail.abstract: This paper describes a discrete-time model of regularly-issued sovereign debt dynamics under a deficit-driven nominal debt growth regime that explicitly accounts for granular maturity. New issuance follows fixed allocations across a finite maturity ladder, and the government budget constraint determines total borrowing endogenously. In the deterministic baseline, we identify a sustainability condition for convergence to a steady-state and derive closed-form steady portfolio shares, as well as key metrics for steady cost and risk (proxied as one-period rollover ratio). Extending the model to a stochastic recurrence equation (SRE) driven by interest rates and (normalized) deficits that are stationary and mean-reverting, and using a future-cashflow state representation of debt, we identify an analogous condition for ergodic convergence to a unique invariant distribution. This implies that metrics calculated by Monte Carlo debt simulations driven by factors with these properties will recover the ergodic means of the under lying system, independently of initial conditions, provided the simulation horizon is sufficiently long. Analytical formulae for expectations of certain key metrics under this invariant distribution are derived, and agreement with simulation is observed. We find that the introduction of stochastic interest-rate/deficit correlation into the framework leads to intuitive correction terms to their deterministic-baseline counterparts.

title: Fairness and the City
affiliations: Hertie School, , Technische Universität Berlin (TU Berlin) and Bochum University of Applied Sciences

detail.title: Fairness and the City
detail.abstract: Fairness perceptions strongly influence public support for policies, especially when their impacts exhibit substantial heterogeneity  across regions, as is the case in urban transport policy. Based on a representative survey of residents in the Berlin-Brandenburg and Paris-Ile-de-France metropolitan regions, we estimate support for different fairness principles and test for place-based resentment between urban and suburban residents. Our analysis shows that 57 percent of metropolitan residents prefer the costs of transport policy to be spread equally across inhabitants, regardless of their proximity to the city centre. Additionally, responses by urban and suburban residents evaluating why a city toll might be unfair also reveal no evidence of place-based resentment.

title: Re reading Saskatchewan in Fiction (1966): Louis “David” Riel, Multiculturalism, and My Early Intellectual Formation (1960s–1980s)

detail.title: Re reading Saskatchewan in Fiction (1966): Louis “David” Riel, Multiculturalism, and My Early Intellectual Formation (1960s–1980s)

detail.abstract: This essay offers a reflective re-examination of Saskatchewan in Fiction (1966) through the intertwined lenses of Louis "David" Riel's contested legacy, the emergence of multiculturalism in Canada, and my own intellectual formation during the 1960s-1980s. Drawing on early academic encounters-including a 1965 undergraduate paper on Riel-I revisit the assumptions, silences, and regional frameworks that shaped mid-century Canadian literary studies. By situating personal experience alongside shifting national discourses, the essay traces how regionalism, Métis history, and multicultural policy converged to influence both the study of Canadian literature and my evolving understanding of cultural identity on the Prairies.

title: UEFA as Referee and Striker: Liberalisation in European Club Football
affiliations: Utrecht University - Utrecht Law School

detail.title: UEFA as Referee and Striker: Liberalisation in European Club Football
detail.abstract: This article examines the evolving regulation of professional football within the European legal order. Sport has gradually become more under the scope of EU law through some landmark judgments. As commercialisation intensifies, the governance structures of professional football in Europe and the legitimacy of UEFA's monopoly position has been increasingly contested, particularly following the European Super League case. UEFA's position in the European club football tournament market does not constitute a natural monopoly in the strict economic sense; instead it exercises a regulatory monopoly by virtue of its power to authorize third-party tournaments. While rival competitions are theoretically possible, UEFA's control over access makes it an gatekeeper in this market similar to gatekeepers in network industries and digital platform economy. Drawing on liberalisation experiences in those two sectors, this article argues that football's regulatory context is distinct due to the specificity of sport. It evaluates third-party access, unbundling and competitive bidding, with the conclusion that the latter offers the best way forward to opening up the European club football tournament market to competition.

title: Challenges of the Power of the New Longevity: Age Discrimination in the Workplace, and More, in Argentina

detail.title: Challenges of the Power of the New Longevity: Age Discrimination in the Workplace, and More, in Argentina
detail.abstract:
Life expectancy has significantly increased, reaching an average of 77 years in Argentina. The current challenge is to enhance the quality of those years. Age discrimination is the third leading cause of discrimination worldwide and is prevalent in Argentina, particularly in workplaces, society, and daily life. Our current challenge is to make those years a life with more quality and fullness. What is the power of all that we have gained and how do we take advantage of it?

The Convention combats ageism, defined as beliefs and norms that justify mistreatment, abuse, or exclusion based on advanced age. 

Global Initiatives and Final Reflection In this sense, the WHO and the UN declared the Decade of Healthy Aging (2021-2030) as a global strategy to promote an inclusive society by changing perceptions of aging. as one of its key pillars. title: Efficient Monte Carlo Valuation of Corporate Bonds in Financial Networks
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - Department of Systems Engineering & Engineering Management and

detail.title: Efficient Monte Carlo Valuation of Corporate Bonds in Financial Networks
detail.abstract: Valuing corporate bonds in systemic economies is challenging due to intricate webs of interinstitutional exposures. When a bank defaults, cascading losses propagate through the network, with payments determined by a system of fixed-point equations lacking closed-form solutions. Standard Monte Carlo methods cannot capture rare yet critical default events, while existing rare-event simulation techniques fail to account for higher-order network effects and scale poorly with network size. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel approach-Bi-Level Importance Sampling with Splitting-and characterize individual bank defaults by decoupling them from the network's complex fixed-point dynamics. This separation enables a two-stage estimation process that directly generates samples from the banks' default events. We demonstrate theoretically that the method is both scalable and asymptotically optimal, and validate its effectiveness through numerical studies on empirically observed networks.

keywords: Women and Children in Armed Conflict

detail.abstract: The Al-Hol camp in northeastern Syria has evolved from a temporary displacement site into a protracted humanitarian and legal crisis hosting more than 80,000 individuals, the majority of whom are women and children. This paper examines Al-Hol as a paradigmatic case of prolonged mass detention in a post-conflict setting, where humanitarian deprivation, security concerns, and unresolved legal status intersect. Drawing on reports from international organizations, human rights bodies, and public health agencies, the study analyzes the camp’s structural deficiencies in sanitation, healthcare, education, and protection, alongside the psychosocial and public health consequences of severe overcrowding and resource scarcity. It further explores how indefinite detention without individualized due process exacerbates vulnerabilities, fuels cycles of trauma, and heightens risks of radicalization, particularly among children deprived of education and social integration. From a legal perspective, the paper assesses compliance with international humanitarian law and international human rights law, including obligations related to humane treatment, the prohibition of collective punishment, and the special protection owed to women and children. The analysis demonstrates that the prevailing security-centric, containment-based approach is neither legally sustainable nor effective in mitigating long-term instability. The paper concludes that durable solutions require a coordinated, rights-based framework centered on individualized legal assessment, rehabilitation, access to essential services, and pathways to reintegration or safe repatriation. Without a decisive shift from indefinite containment to lawful and humane resolution mechanisms, Al-Hol risks entrenching a generational humanitarian, legal, and security failure with consequences extending well beyond northeastern Syria.

title: GDP Forecast of the Biggest GCC Economies using ARIMA
affiliations: European Centre for Economic Studies of the Arab Orient, Beirut Arab University, Economics Department, Lebanon and Beirut Arab University

detail.title: GDP Forecast of the Biggest GCC Economies using ARIMA
detail.abstract: Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) members are considered one of the fastest growing economies. This paper aims to empirically forecast the economic activity of the vastest GCC countries: Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. An Auto-Regressive Moving Average (ARIMA) model for the three countries Gross Domestic Product is obtained using the Box-Jenkins methodology during the 1980-2020 period. The appropriate models for the three economies are of ARIMA (0,2,1), the forecasts are at a 95% confidence level and predicts a growth in the three countries for the upcoming five years.

title: Intertemporal Competition and Rotation
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics, , University of Science and Technology of China (USTC) and Duke University - Fuqua School of Business

detail.title: Intertemporal Competition and Rotation
detail.abstract: Does competition happen only when multiple agents work simultaneously? This paper shows that it may be more efficient to leverage competition when agents are not working together. Consider a principal trying to motivate agents to exert effort in order to achieve an innovation breakthrough, modeled as a Poisson arrival. The instantaneous arrival rate of the breakthrough is concave increasing in the total effort levels of all agents. We show that motivating more than one agent to work simultaneously is sub-optimal. Instead, a rotation contract is asymptotically optimal. Rotation creates a sense of urgency for each agent, which reduces the rent the principal has to pay for the effort. To make the contract more practical, we also study a One-Shot contract structure. Despite its simplicity, this contract performs extremely well. It achieves at least 94% of the optimal payoff in a symmetric two-agent setting, and converges to optimality when the number of available agents grows to infinity.

title: Use-specific Storage Premia and Market Stabilization for Critical Minerals in the Presence of Geopolitical Risk
affiliations: , Monash University - Department of Economics, University of Tasmania - School of Economics and Finance and Monash Business School

detail.title: Use-specific Storage Premia and Market Stabilization for Critical Minerals in the Presence of Geopolitical Risk
detail.abstract: This paper examines how geopolitical risk affects metal prices and stockpiling when demand is unevenly distributed across end uses. We develop a Theory of Use-Specific Storage Premia, which posits that demand concentration and limited redeployability raise effective storage costs and weaken the stabilizing role of inventories/stockpiling. Using deterioration in United States-China political relations as a shock to forward-looking demand expectations, we estimate price and inventory responses for metals with well-established markets. Broad-use metals exhibit significant price declines and precautionary stockpiling following geopolitical deterioration, while use-specific metals display muted responses. Cross-sectional evidence links these patterns directly to use-specificity. The results imply that traditional stockpiling is structurally less effective for battery-linked critical minerals subject to geopolitical risk.
