detail.abstract:
Organisations are approving AI-assisted decisions they cannot defend under scrutiny. These systems perform fluently. They do not verify. That distinction is architectural. Verification debt begins here: decisions are taken on outputs that cannot be intrinsically verified at the point of generation. Performance is treated as reliability and compliance as defensibility. Neither holds once justification is demanded under compulsion.

This paper introduces the KEV governance framework and the minimum conditions for defensible AI decision-making when verification is absent by construction (V = 0). It is written for boards, regulators, auditors and legal practitioners operating where AI-assisted reasoning already shapes decisions carrying fiduciary, regulatory and litigation consequence.

It shows how verification absence migrates into organisations as unverified assumptions embedded in material decisions, accumulating as latent liability until a regulator, court, auditor or counterparty demands reconstruction. It specifies an enforcement model – the Sovereign Intelligence Flywheel – defining evidentiary standards, verification authority, independent reconstruction requirements and manual pathway preservation sufficient to survive hostile examination. The framework exposes accountability arbitrage: capturing efficiency gains by removing human decision-makers while liability concentrates at board level unchecked.

Six modular appendices translate the framework into protocols for boards, procurement, investor due diligence and audit, each usable independently. The paper maps how verification absence converts into measurable capital impairment: asset writedowns, transaction discounting, insurance exclusion and audit qualification across organisations sharing common architectural substrates.

The framework is deliberately falsifiable. If a system demonstrates intrinsic, consequence-bearing verification independent of human reconstruction, the constraint described here ceases to apply. No widely deployed foundation model architecture currently satisfies that condition. Where these conditions are not met and AI-assisted decisions carry legal, financial or board-level consequence, the act of approval itself becomes the liability event.

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) such as GitHub Copilot are increasingly deployed not merely to assist developers with code completion, but to perform large-scale automated code migration-converting entire legacy codebases from one language and framework to another. In regulated financial services, where software systems manage sensitive instruments such as employee stock option plans, loan servicing platforms, and trading infrastructure, this practice introduces a distinct and underexplored set of ethical challenges at the intersection of AI ethics, software engineering, and financial regulation. This paper examines the ethical dimensions of AI-assisted code migration within enterprise financial systems, drawing on firsthand practitioner experience deploying LLM-driven conversion workflows at a major financial institution. Three core ethical tensions are identified: an accountability gap when AI-generated code fails in production, a transparency deficit that impedes regulatory audit and compliance verification, and an automation bias that leads teams to place unwarranted trust in AI-converted code. A practitioner-grounded ethical framework is proposed, consisting of mandatory human review checkpoints, provenance documentation for AI-generated components, and differential testing protocols that verify functional equivalence against original systems. This work moves beyond abstract ethical principles toward actionable guidance rooted in the realities of enterprise software engineering, and calls on industry leaders, compliance teams, and AI tool providers to co-develop standardized ethical review processes for AI-generated code in regulated industries.

detail.abstract: We reveal three points why econometrics and economic theory can't help to select an optimal portfolio. 1. We show that Markowitz' variance describes only a limited market case when all trade volumes are assumed constant. The use of this approximation while predicting the portfolio variance, which depends on random trade volumes, is like the use of constant steps while forecasting random Brownian walks. We overcome this limitation and derive the market-based variance that depends on covariances of random values and volumes of trades with portfolio securities. That ties up the predictions of portfolio variance with the forecasts of the time series of trade values and volumes. 2. Markowitz considered the forecast of the variance at horizon T as a measure of market risks that returns may deviate from the predicted mean return and that may cause losses. We point to the existence of the 2 nd-order market risks, which are missed now, that at horizon T the variance may deviate from the predicted variance, like how returns may deviate from the predicted mean return. If so, returns at horizon T may deviate from the predicted mean return more than is predicted by the variance forecast, and that may increase the losses. We introduce the measure of the 2 nd-order risks, which depends on the 4 th statistical moments of values and volumes of market trades. The accounting for two market risks substantially complicates portfolio selection. 3. We show that modern econometrics and theoretical economics can't justify the accurate and reliable predictions of the portfolio variance. The forecasts of the 2 nd-order market risk's measure are all the more beyond the prediction capabilities of modern economics. Without economically justified forecasts of market risks, the optimal portfolio selection becomes an investing belle art of empirical anticipations multiplied by the power of AI methods.

detail.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) disruption reshapes value distribution across semiconductor supply chains, challenging traditional "smiling curve" assumptions that predict manufacturing commands premium valuations. Analyzing 136 firms across Taiwan and the United States (1986-2025), we document an extreme U-shaped value distribution where ecosystem-controlling Apex firms (IC designers, IP licensors) capture valuations 12.4 times higher than capital-intensive Midstream manufacturers (foundries, IDMs) in the U.S. market and 6.2 times higher in Taiwan. Leveraging ChatGPT's November 2022 launch as a natural experiment, difference-indifferences analysis establishes causal evidence that AI demand shocks amplify pre-existing asymmetries: Apex firms gained +65.7% in Tobin's Q while Midstream declined-18.8%, an 84.6 percentage point divergence. detail.abstract: This paper describes the Quarterly Macro Forecasting Framework (QMFF), which is a novel approach to macroeconomic policy analysis and forecasting. At the core of this framework is a Quarterly Projection Model, with main behavioral equations quantified as deviations of real variables from their trends. The model comprises a simultaneous system of calibrated equations that cover the main sectors of the Financial Programming and Policies framework, as well as key accounting restrictions within and across sectors. By explicitly accounting for trends observed in real variables and relative prices, the framework ensures a balanced growth path and constant expenditure shares relative to nominal GDP. The QMFF is sufficiently flexible to be adapted to different monetary frameworks and exchange rate regimes. After describing the framework, the paper illustrates its implementation for policy analysis and forecasting on the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The empirical work with the model includes not only calibration but also testing the model’s dynamic and in-sample simulation properties.

detail.abstract: Capital flow restrictions have long been debated as a tool to manage external financial vulnerabilities, as volatile international capital flows and high external debt can contribute to financial crises. However, empirical evidence on whether capital flow management measures (CFMs) can shift the composition of countries’ external liabilities toward more stable types of funding is limited. Using a novel dataset of granular capital account openness indicators measuring policy intensity, we show that an asymmetric liberalization favoring equity over debt can tilt external capital structures toward equity. This effect is stronger in countries with higher institutional quality, underscoring the role of governance in attracting stable foreign investment.

affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Cadasters, Asset Tangibility, and Growth

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Cadasters—records of land and property ownership—constitute an important pillar of a country’s institutional landscape by enabling the assignment of property rights. This paper examines the impact of cadasters on long-term economic growth by identifying a specific channel in this link: asset tangibility. It hypothesizes that the more a firm’s assets are tangible, the more relevant cadasters become. The analysis uses a cross-country dataset on cadasters together with granular data from industry panels over the last six decades. The results show that the development of cadasters fosters long-term growth, particularly in industries with high asset tangibility. Higher investment in those industries, resulting from stronger cadasters, contributes to this pattern. The growth impact of cadasters is more pronounced in (i) countries that lack strong cadasters, such as in Sub-Saharan Africa; and (ii) countries with typically more investment-conducive legal systems. The findings suggest that cadastral reforms can help stimulate investment and sustain long-term growth in many developing economies.

detail.abstract: In a canonical model of policy formation, campaign contributions, and electoral competition, we show that, despite donor polarization, candidates’ agendas converge. If purely office-motivated candidates move away from the centrist agenda, they increase their opponents’ contributions more than their own. An extension that introduces a “job ladder” for the candidates leads to candidates caring about absolute levels of campaign contributions and generates divergence of political agendas in equilibrium. We provide empirical evidence of campaign contributions affecting candidates’ chances of “promotion,” and characterize key comparative statics of the extended model. In the model, caps on campaign contributions lower polarization in equilibrium.

detail.title: How Effectively Can Current LLMs Analyze Macrofinancial Issues?

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper empirically evaluates the ability of current Large Language Models (LLMs) to analyze macrofinancial coverage in IMF Article IV staff reports, using human economists' assessments as a benchmark. We test several GPT models on reports from 2016-2024, assessing their performance on both qualitative ratings and binary questions. Our findings indicate that the latest models can meaningfully assist economists, achieving an average accuracy of 71-75% on ratings and an average exact match rate of 76-81% on binary questions in 2024 across advanced GPT models. However, we find that LLMs tend to assign higher, less-dispersed ratings than human experts and struggle with open-ended questions that require deep contextual judgment. The paper provides quantitative evidence on current LLM accuracy in this domain, explores the drivers of its performance, and discusses key limitations such as optimistic bias.
